title: Νὺξ καὶ πυρά
titleEn: Night and the Watch-Fires of Troy — Iliad 8.469–565
part: Night and the Watch-Fires of Troy (8.469–565)
about: Zeus answers Hera’s submission with a prophecy: at dawn she will see him destroying still more of the Argive army, and Hector will not stop fighting until Achilles rises up beside the ships over the dead Patroclus. He adds that he cares nothing for her anger, though she go to the world’s end. The sun sets, welcome to the Achaeans and unwelcome to the Trojans. Hector calls an assembly on open ground by the river and says that darkness alone has saved the Achaeans; he orders supper, fires all night, and watchers on the walls, and promises to test Diomedes at dawn. The Trojans do as he says, though the gods refuse their sacrifice, and a thousand fires burn on the plain like stars around the moon, with the horses waiting beside their chariots for Dawn.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: Zeus now replies to Hera, who ended the last part by giving way. The whole line is the usual speech introduction: ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, προσέφη ‘addressed’ is an aorist of πρόσφημι, and νεφεληγερέτα ‘cloud-gatherer’ is the nominative of Zeus’ stock epithet, ending in -α as ἱππότα does. The line stands in the same words at 1.560.

sentences.t:
ἠοῦς δὴ καὶ μᾶλλον ὑπερμενέα Κρονίωνα
ὄψεαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα, βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη
ὀλλύντ’ Ἀργείων πουλὺν στρατὸν αἰχμητάων·
sentences.i: “At dawn, ox-eyed lady Hera, if you wish, you will see the son of Cronus, of surpassing strength, destroying still more of the great army of the Argive spearmen;
sentences.n: Zeus’ answer opens with a prophecy, in which he calls himself ‘the son of Cronus’. ἠοῦς ‘at dawn’ is a genitive of time, and καὶ μᾶλλον ‘still more’ is best taken with ὀλλύντ’ (for ὀλλύντα), ‘destroying still more’, though the order lets it be read earlier. ὑπερμενέα ‘of surpassing strength’ and βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ are stock epithets. ὄψεαι is the future of ὁράω with its vowels left open, and ἐθέλῃσθα is the subjunctive with the ending -σθα. πουλύν is πολύν, and αἰχμητάων is the epic genitive plural.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πρὶν πολέμου ἀποπαύσεται ὄβριμος Ἕκτωρ
πρὶν ὄρθαι παρὰ ναῦφι ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα,
ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ ἂν οἳ μὲν ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσι μάχωνται
στείνει ἐν αἰνοτάτῳ περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος·
sentences.i: For mighty Hector will not stop fighting before the fleet-footed son of Peleus rises up beside the ships, on that day when the men fight at the sterns, in a most dreadful strait, about the dead Patroclus;
sentences.n: The reason for the prophecy. Πηλεΐωνα ‘the son of Peleus’ is Achilles, who is not named, and ποδώκεα ‘fleet-footed’ is his epithet here. ὄρθαι is an infinitive of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’ in an old aorist form, with the sense ‘rise up’; ναῦφι has the ending -φι (‘by the ships’). ὅτ’ ἂν … μάχωνται is ‘on the day when they shall fight’, with the subjunctive. στείνει is a dative of στεῖνος ‘narrow place’, and αἰνοτάτῳ is the superlative of αἰνός ‘dread’. Πατρόκλοιο is the epic genitive.

sentences.t: ὣς γὰρ θέσφατόν ἐστι·
sentences.l: for so it is god-declared;
sentences.i: for so it is decreed;
sentences.n: ὣς γάρ ‘for so’ says that what has just been foretold is already fixed. θέσφατον, a neuter adjective used as a predicate, is what a god has declared (θεός and the root of φημί): a decree or fate. It is not the same word as μοῖρα ‘fate’. The unit ends in the middle of the line, and the next begins with a new clause.

sentences.t:
σέθεν δ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀλεγίζω
χωομένης, οὐδ’ εἴ κε τὰ νείατα πείραθ’ ἵκηαι
γαίης καὶ πόντοιο,
sentences.l:
but of you I do not care,
you being incensed, not even if the lowest limits you reach
of earth and open-sea,
sentences.i: but I do not care about you, incensed as you are, not even if you reach the lowest limits of earth and sea,
sentences.n: Zeus brushes off Hera’s anger. σέθεν δ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀλεγίζω ‘but of you I do not care’ is the phrase Agamemnon uses to Achilles at 1.180, with σέθεν the epic genitive of σύ, governed by the verb; χωομένης is a genitive participle of χώομαι ‘be incensed’, ‘you being incensed’. οὐδ’ εἴ κε … ἵκηαι is ‘not even if you reach’, ἵκηαι being the second-person subjunctive middle with the epic ending -ηαι. πείραθα ‘limits’ is the old plural of πεῖραρ.

sentences.t:
ἵν’ Ἰάπετός τε Κρόνος τε
ἥμενοι οὔτ’ αὐγῇς Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο
τέρποντ’ οὔτ’ ἀνέμοισι, βαθὺς δέ τε Τάρταρος ἀμφίς·
sentences.i: where Iapetus and Cronus sit, taking delight neither in the rays of Hyperion the Sun nor in any winds, and deep Tartarus lies all about them;
sentences.n: The farthest place Zeus can think of: Tartarus, where the old gods Iapetus and Cronus, Zeus’ own father, sit. ἵνα here is ‘where’; ἥμενοι is ‘sitting’; τέρποντ’ is τέρπονται, ‘take delight’, followed by the genitive αὐγῇς ‘glare, bright light’ and the dative ἀνέμοισι ‘in winds’. Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο is ‘Hyperion the Sun’, Hyperion being a name of the sun-god, in apposition. The old genitive -οιο is Homeric; ἀμφίς is ‘all round’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἢν ἔνθ’ ἀφίκηαι ἀλωμένη, οὔ σευ ἔγωγε
σκυζομένης ἀλέγω, ἐπεὶ οὐ σέο κύντερον ἄλλο.
sentences.l:
Not even if you come there, wandering, not of you, I at least,
being sullen, do I care, since than you there is nothing else more dog-like.”
sentences.i: Not even if you wander off to that place will I care about your sullen mood, for there is nothing else more shameless than you.”
sentences.n: The close of Zeus’ speech, and its sharpest word. ἀφίκηαι is the subjunctive (‘if you come’) and ἀλωμένη ‘wandering’ agrees with Hera; σευ is the epic genitive of σύ, governed by ἀλέγω ‘care for’, and σκυζομένης is the genitive participle of σκύζομαι ‘be sullen’. κύντερον is the comparative of κύων ‘dog’, ‘more dog-like’, and a dog stands for shamelessness. ἐπεὶ οὐ σέο κύντερον ἄλλο is ‘since nothing else is more dog-like than you’.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη λευκώλενος Ἥρη.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him not at all addressed white-armed Hera.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and white-armed Hera said nothing to him.
sentences.n: Hera does not reply. The line is the usual ‘so he spoke … X addressed him’ turned round: οὔ τι ‘not at all’ negates προσέφη ‘addressed’, so that the formula that introduces a speech here reports none. λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is her stock epithet. In the previous part she had given way to Zeus’ threat and stayed out of the fighting, and she is now silent.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἔπεσ’ Ὠκεανῷ λαμπρὸν φάος ἠελίοιο
ἕλκον νύκτα μέλαιναν ἐπὶ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν.
sentences.l:
And fell into Oceanus the bright light of the sun,
dragging black night over the grain-giving plough-land.
sentences.i: The bright light of the sun fell into Oceanus, drawing dark night over the grain-giving plough-land.
sentences.n: Sunset ends the day’s fighting. ἐν δ’ ἔπεσ’ is ἐν … ἔπεσε with the preposition set apart from its verb (tmesis), ‘fell in’; Ὠκεανῷ is the dative, Oceanus being the great river that is thought to circle the earth. λαμπρὸν φάος ἠελίοιο ‘the bright light of the sun’ is a stock phrase for the sun itself. ἕλκον is the neuter participle agreeing with φάος, ‘dragging’. ζείδωρον ἄρουραν ‘the grain-giving plough-land’ is a stock phrase for the earth.

sentences.t:
Τρωσὶν μέν ῥ’ ἀέκουσιν ἔδυ φάος, αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοῖς
ἀσπασίη τρίλλιστος ἐπήλυθε νὺξ ἐρεβεννή.
sentences.l:
To the Trojans, then, unwilling, the light went down, but to the Achaeans
welcome, thrice-prayed-for, came the murky night.
sentences.i: The light set against the will of the Trojans, but to the Achaeans the murky night came welcome, thrice prayed for.
sentences.n: Night means opposite things to the two armies. μέν ῥ’ is μέν ῥά, a particle pair setting Τρωσίν against Ἀχαιοῖς; ἀέκουσιν is ‘unwilling’ in the dative, and ἔδυ ‘went down’ is the aorist of δύω. ἀσπασίη ‘welcome’ and τρίλλιστος agree with νύξ; τρίλλιστος is from λίσσομαι ‘pray’, ‘prayed for’, and the τρι- may mean ‘three times’ or only ‘much’. ἐπήλυθε is the aorist of ἐπέρχομαι, and ἐρεβεννή is ‘murky’.

sentences.t:
Τρώων αὖτ’ ἀγορὴν ποιήσατο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
νόσφι νεῶν ἀγαγὼν ποταμῷ ἔπι δινήεντι,
ἐν καθαρῷ ὅθι δὴ νεκύων διεφαίνετο χῶρος.
sentences.l:
Of the Trojans again an assembly made glorious Hector,
apart from the ships, having led them to the eddying river,
in a clean place, where indeed of the dead the ground showed through.
sentences.i: Glorious Hector, in his turn, held an assembly of the Trojans, leading them away from the ships to the eddying river, to a clear place where the ground showed through, free of the dead.
sentences.n: A new scene, a Trojan assembly. Τρώων is the genitive after ἀγορήν ‘assembly’, and ποιήσατο is the middle of ποιέω, ‘made for himself’, so ‘held’; αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again, in turn’. νόσφι νεῶν is ‘apart from the ships’, and ἔπι with its accent drawn back means ‘at’ the river. ἐν καθαρῷ is ‘in a clear (clean) place’, and νεκύων διεφαίνετο χῶρος ‘the place of the dead showed through’ is usually taken to mean open ground, free of corpses, though the genitive could also mean ‘among the dead’.

sentences.t:
ἐξ ἵππων δ’ ἀποβάντες ἐπὶ χθόνα μῦθον ἄκουον
τόν ῥ’ Ἕκτωρ ἀγόρευε Διῒ φίλος·
sentences.l:
And from their horses having stepped down, onto the ground the word they listened to
which Hector declared, dear to Zeus;
sentences.i: They stepped down from their horses to the ground and listened to the speech that Hector, dear to Zeus, declared;
sentences.n: ἐξ ἵππων ‘from the horses’ means from the horse-drawn chariots, which is how heroes ride to a meeting. ἀποβάντες is the aorist participle of ἀποβαίνω ‘step down’, and ἄκουον ‘were listening to’ takes the accusative μῦθον. τόν ῥ’ is τὸν ῥά, with τόν a relative pronoun, ‘which’; ἀγόρευε is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘declare’, a public address. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ is Hector’s stock epithet here, the dative of Ζεύς with the diaeresis marked.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα χειρὶ
ἔγχος ἔχ’ ἑνδεκάπηχυ· πάροιθε δὲ λάμπετο δουρὸς
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη, περὶ δὲ χρύσεος θέε πόρκης,
sentences.l:
and in his hand
a spear he held, eleven-cubit; and in front gleamed of the spear
the point, bronze, and around it ran a golden ring,
sentences.i: and in his hand he held a spear eleven cubits long; and the bronze point of the spear gleamed in front, and a golden ring ran round it,
sentences.n: Hector’s spear, described in the same words as at 6.318–320. ἔχ’ is ἔχε, the imperfect ‘held’; ἑνδεκάπηχυ is ‘eleven-cubit’, a cubit being the length of a forearm, and ἔγχος is a spear. The next clause repeats the words of 6.319–320: λάμπετο ‘gleamed’, with αἰχμή ‘point’ in the nominative and the genitive δουρός ‘of the spear’ depending on it, and θέε ‘ran’ with the ring πόρκης (a band round the head of the spear). The ‘golden ring’ is the nominative χρύσεος … πόρκης.

sentences.t: τῷ ὅ γ’ ἐρεισάμενος ἔπεα Τρώεσσι μετηύδα·
sentences.l: On this leaning, he spoke words among the Trojans:
sentences.i: Leaning on it, he spoke words among the Trojans:
sentences.n: τῷ is the spear (dative ‘on it’), and ὅ γε is ‘he’. ἐρεισάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρείδω ‘prop, press’, ‘having propped himself’: Hector speaks leaning on his spear. μετηύδα is the imperfect of μεταυδάω ‘speak among’, with the dative Τρώεσσι (the epic -εσσι ending). The colon opens Hector’s speech, which runs to 541.

sentences.t: κέκλυτέ μευ Τρῶες καὶ Δάρδανοι ἠδ’ ἐπίκουροι·
sentences.l: “Hear me, Trojans and Dardanians and allies;
sentences.i: “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians and allies;
sentences.n: Hector’s speech begins with the call for attention heard at 3.456. κέκλυτε is the reduplicated imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, with μευ, the epic genitive ‘me’. Δάρδανοι are the Dardanians, a people allied with the Trojans, and ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’ are the foreign troops who have come to fight for Troy. The ἠδ’ is ἠδέ ‘and’.

sentences.t:
νῦν ἐφάμην νῆάς τ’ ὀλέσας καὶ πάντας Ἀχαιοὺς
ἂψ ἀπονοστήσειν προτὶ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν·
sentences.l:
Just now I thought, having destroyed the ships and all the Achaeans,
that back I would return to windy Ilios;
sentences.i: I thought just now that I would destroy the ships and all the Achaeans and go back to windy Ilios;
sentences.n: Hector says what he had hoped for the day. ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle of φημί ‘say, think’, with the future infinitive ἀπονοστήσειν ‘that I would return home’; νῦν is ‘just now’ (or ‘by now’), and ὀλέσας is the aorist participle of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’. Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν ‘windy Ilios’ is a stock phrase, with the accusative after προτί (= πρός).

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πρὶν κνέφας ἦλθε, τὸ νῦν ἐσάωσε μάλιστα
Ἀργείους καὶ νῆας ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
but before that, darkness came, which now has saved most of all
the Argives and the ships on the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: But darkness came first, and it is that which has now saved the Argives and their ships on the shore where the sea breaks, above all.
sentences.n: The reason he has to stop. πρίν here is ‘before’ without a verb after it, ‘but before that happened’, and κνέφας ‘darkness’ is the subject of ἦλθε. τό is the relative ‘which’ (the article-form used as a relative), ἐσάωσε is the aorist of σαόω, the epic form of σώζω ‘save’, and μάλιστα ‘most of all’ goes with it. ῥηγμῖνι is the dative of ῥηγμίν ‘the place where the sea breaks’, the beach.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι νῦν μὲν πειθώμεθα νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ
δόρπά τ’ ἐφοπλισόμεσθα·
sentences.l:
But indeed for now let us obey black night
and prepare our supper;
sentences.i: But for now, indeed, let us yield to dark night and prepare our supper;
sentences.n: Hector turns to the night’s tasks. πειθώμεθα is a subjunctive of urging (‘let us obey’, put in English as ‘let us yield to’), with the dative νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ ‘black night’; ἤτοι is one word as the edition prints it. ἐφοπλισόμεσθα, from ἐφοπλίζω ‘make ready’, can be read as a short-vowel subjunctive ‘let us prepare’ or as a future ‘we shall prepare’; ‘let us’ suits the surrounding appeals. δόρπα is the plural of δόρπον ‘supper’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ καλλίτριχας ἵππους
λύσαθ’ ὑπὲξ ὀχέων, παρὰ δέ σφισι βάλλετ’ ἐδωδήν·
sentences.l:
and the fair-maned horses
unyoke from the chariots, and beside them throw food;
sentences.i: and unyoke the fair-maned horses from the chariots, and throw them food;
sentences.n: Orders for the horses. ἀτάρ is ‘and, but’, and καλλίτριχας ‘fair-maned’ is the Odyssey’s epithet for horses. λύσαθ’ is the aorist active imperative of λύω, ‘unyoke’ (λύσατε, with τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ὑπέξ); ὑπὲξ is ‘out from under’, with the genitive ὀχέων ‘the chariots’. παρὰ δέ … βάλλετ’ separates the preposition from the verb (tmesis), ‘throw beside’, with σφισι ‘for them’ and ἐδωδήν ‘food’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ πόλιος δ’ ἄξεσθε βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα
καρπαλίμως, οἶνον δὲ μελίφρονα οἰνίζεσθε
σῖτόν τ’ ἐκ μεγάρων, ἐπὶ δὲ ξύλα πολλὰ λέγεσθε,
sentences.l:
and from the city bring for yourselves cattle and stout flocks
swiftly, and wine, honey-hearted, get for yourselves,
and food from the halls, and much wood gather besides,
sentences.i: and bring cattle and stout flocks from the city, swiftly, and get yourselves heart-sweetening wine and food from the halls, and gather plenty of wood besides,
sentences.n: Supplies for the night. ἄξεσθε is the aorist middle imperative of ἄγω, ‘bring for yourselves’; ἴφια μῆλα ‘stout flocks’ are sheep and goats, as in the Odyssey. μελίφρονα ‘honey-hearted’ is the wine’s stock epithet (sense uncertain), and οἰνίζεσθε ‘get yourselves wine’ is a verb made from οἶνος. σῖτον is grain or food, and μεγάρων are the halls or houses of the city. ἐπὶ δὲ … λέγεσθε is ‘and gather besides’, with the preposition set apart.

sentences.t:
ὥς κεν παννύχιοι μέσφ’ ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης
καίωμεν πυρὰ πολλά, σέλας δ’ εἰς οὐρανὸν ἵκῃ,
sentences.l:
so that all night long, until early-born dawn,
we may burn many fires, and the gleam may reach heaven,
sentences.i: so that all night long, until early-born dawn, we may keep many fires burning, and their gleam may reach heaven,
sentences.n: The purpose of the wood: ὥς κεν with the subjunctive gives ‘so that we may’. παννύχιοι ‘all night long’ agrees with the subject, μέσφ’ ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης is ‘until early-born dawn’ (the epithet is the Odyssey’s for Dawn), and καίωμεν is the subjunctive of καίω ‘burn’. πυρά is the plural of πῦρ, ‘fires’. σέλας ‘gleam’ is a light, here the glow of many fires; ἵκῃ is the subjunctive ‘may reach’.

sentences.t:
μή πως καὶ διὰ νύκτα κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
φεύγειν ὁρμήσωνται ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
lest in any way even through the night the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
set out to flee over the broad back of the sea.
sentences.i: lest the long-haired Achaeans somehow set out to flee, even through the night, over the sea’s broad back.
sentences.n: Why the fires are needed: Hector fears that the Achaeans will slip away in the dark. μή πως … ὁρμήσωνται is a clause of fear, ‘lest in some way they set out’, with the aorist subjunctive. κάρη κομόωντες ‘long-haired’ (literally ‘with hair on their heads’) is the stock epithet of the Achaeans. ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης ‘over the broad back of the sea’ is a stock phrase of the poem, and νῶτα is plural.

sentences.t: μὴ μὰν ἀσπουδί γε νεῶν ἐπιβαῖεν ἕκηλοι,
sentences.l: Let them not, in truth, board their ships without effort, at ease,
sentences.i: Let them not, in truth, go aboard their ships without any trouble, at their ease,
sentences.n: μὴ μάν is ‘let them not, in truth’, and ἐπιβαῖεν, an aorist optative, is a wish or prohibition, ‘may they not board’, with the genitive νεῶν. ἀσπουδί is made from the negative ἀ- and σπουδή ‘haste, effort’, ‘without effort or trouble’, and ἕκηλοι ‘at ease, undisturbed’ agrees with the subject. The sentence goes on in the next unit: they must not leave unhurt.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὥς τις τούτων γε βέλος καὶ οἴκοθι πέσσῃ
βλήμενος ἢ ἰῷ ἢ ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι
νηὸς ἐπιθρῴσκων,
sentences.l:
but so that someone of them, at least, even at home may digest a shaft,
struck by an arrow or by a sharp spear
leaping onto his ship,
sentences.i: but so that someone among them, at least, may nurse the hurt of a shaft even at home, struck by an arrow or a sharp spear as he leaps aboard his ship,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὥς is ‘but so that’, with the subjunctive πέσσῃ. πέσσω is ‘cook, digest’, used of brooding over or enduring something; so ‘digest a shaft’ is ‘have a wound to nurse’. οἴκοθι is ‘at home’. βλήμενος is the aorist participle of βάλλω, ‘struck’, with ἰῷ ‘arrow’ and ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι ‘sharp spear’ in the dative; νηὸς ἐπιθρῴσκων is ‘leaping onto a ship’, with the genitive.

sentences.t:
ἵνα τις στυγέῃσι καὶ ἄλλος
Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοισι φέρειν πολύδακρυν Ἄρηα.
sentences.l:
so that someone else too may loathe
to bring upon the horse-taming Trojans tearful Ares.
sentences.i: so that another also may hate to bring tearful battle upon the Trojans, tamers of horses.
sentences.n: ἵνα … στυγέῃσι is ‘so that … may hate’, with the epic subjunctive ending -σι; στυγέω with an infinitive is ‘shrink from doing’, as at 1.186–187. τις … καὶ ἄλλος is ‘someone else too’. Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοισι is ‘upon the Trojans, tamers of horses’, the stock epithet. πολύδακρυν ‘tearful’ (πολύ ‘much’ and δάκρυ ‘tear’) belongs to Ἄρηα, the war-god’s name standing for battle.

sentences.t:
κήρυκες δ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ Διῒ φίλοι ἀγγελλόντων
παῖδας πρωθήβας πολιοκροτάφους τε γέροντας
λέξασθαι περὶ ἄστυ θεοδμήτων ἐπὶ πύργων·
sentences.i: And let heralds, dear to Zeus, go through the town and proclaim that boys in early youth and grey-templed old men are to lie down round the town on the towers built by the gods;
sentences.n: More orders: ἀγγελλόντων is a third-person plural imperative, ‘let them announce’, with ἀνὰ ἄστυ ‘through the town’; Διῒ φίλοι ‘dear to Zeus’ is a stock epithet of heralds. The message is an indirect statement with an infinitive: παῖδας πρωθήβας ‘boys in first youth’ and πολιοκροτάφους … γέροντας ‘old men grey at the temples’ are to λέξασθαι, aorist middle of λέγω, ‘lie down’ (to keep watch). θεοδμήτων ‘god-built’ refers to the towers of Troy.

sentences.t:
θηλύτεραι δὲ γυναῖκες ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἑκάστη
πῦρ μέγα καιόντων·
sentences.l:
and the female women, in the halls, each one,
a great fire let burn;
sentences.i: and let the women, each in her hall, keep a great fire burning;
sentences.n: θηλύτεραι is the comparative of θῆλυς ‘female’, used here without any comparison, so that ‘the female women’ means simply ‘the women’, as in the Odyssey. ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν is ‘in the halls’ and ἑκάστη ‘each one’ is feminine singular. καιόντων is a third-person plural imperative of καίω, ‘let them burn’; πῦρ μέγα ‘a great fire’ is the object. The women’s task is a second fire in every house, behind the fires on the field.

sentences.t:
φυλακὴ δέ τις ἔμπεδος ἔστω
μὴ λόχος εἰσέλθῃσι πόλιν λαῶν ἀπεόντων.
sentences.l:
and let there be some firm watch,
lest an ambush enter the city, the people being away.
sentences.i: and let there be a firm watch, lest an ambush enter the city while the troops are away.
sentences.n: φυλακή is ‘a watch’ and τις ‘some’; ἔμπεδος ‘firm’ agrees with it. ἔστω is the third-person imperative of εἰμί. μὴ … εἰσέλθῃσι is a negative purpose clause, ‘lest an ambush come in’, with the aorist subjunctive, and λόχος ‘ambush’ is the subject. λαῶν ἀπεόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘the people being away’, meaning the army out of the city at the ships.

sentences.t: ὧδ’ ἔστω Τρῶες μεγαλήτορες ὡς ἀγορεύω·
sentences.l: Thus let it be, great-spirited Trojans, as I declare;
sentences.i: Let it be so, great-spirited Trojans, as I declare it;
sentences.n: ὧδ’ is ὧδε ‘thus’, and ἔστω ‘let it be’ confirms the whole set of orders. Τρῶες μεγαλήτορες ‘great-spirited Trojans’ is a vocative with a stock epithet (the Odyssey’s μεγαλήτωρ). ὡς ἀγορεύω is ‘as I declare’, ἀγορεύω being the verb of public speaking; this is Hector closing his list of orders.

sentences.t:
μῦθος δ’ ὃς μὲν νῦν ὑγιὴς εἰρημένος ἔστω,
τὸν δ’ ἠοῦς Τρώεσσι μεθ’ ἱπποδάμοις ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.l:
and the speech which now, sound, has been spoken, let it stand,
but that one at dawn among the horse-taming Trojans I will declare.
sentences.i: As for the word that has now been spoken, let it stand as sound; the other word I shall declare at dawn among the Trojans, tamers of horses.
sentences.n: ὃς μὲν νῦν … τὸν δ’ ἠοῦς sets a speech ‘now’ against a speech ‘at dawn’: the first word is what he has just said, the second one he will say tomorrow. εἰρημένος is the perfect passive participle (εἴρημαι, the perfect that serves λέγω), and with ἔστω ‘let it be’ it makes ‘let it have been said’, and ὑγιής ‘sound’ (literally ‘healthy’) is its predicate. ἠοῦς is a genitive of time, ‘at dawn’; ἀγορεύσω is the future of ἀγορεύω. Τρώεσσι μεθ’ ἱπποδάμοις is ‘among the Trojans, tamers of horses’.

sentences.t:
ἔλπομαι εὐχόμενος Διί τ’ ἄλλοισίν τε θεοῖσιν
ἐξελάαν ἐνθένδε κύνας κηρεσσιφορήτους,
οὓς κῆρες φορέουσι μελαινάων ἐπὶ νηῶν.
sentences.l:
I hope, praying to Zeus and to the other gods,
to drive out from here dogs borne by death-spirits,
whom death-spirits carry on black ships.
sentences.i: I hope, in my prayer to Zeus and the other gods, to drive out from here the dogs borne by the spirits of death, whom the spirits of death carry on black ships.
sentences.n: Hector looks to tomorrow. ἔλπομαι εὐχόμενος is ‘I hope, praying’, with the infinitive ἐξελάαν ‘to drive out’ (ἐξελαύνω). The ‘dogs’ are the Achaeans, called dogs in scorn; κηρεσσιφορήτους is made from κῆρες ‘death-spirits’ and φορέω ‘carry’, ‘carried by death-spirits’, and the relative clause repeats the idea: κῆρες φορέουσι ‘spirits of death bear them’ on μελαινάων … νηῶν ‘black ships’, the genitive plural with the epic ending -άων.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι ἐπὶ νυκτὶ φυλάξομεν ἡμέας αὐτούς,
πρῶϊ δ’ ὑπηοῖοι σὺν τεύχεσι θωρηχθέντες
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐγείρομεν ὀξὺν Ἄρηα.
sentences.l:
But indeed for the night we will keep guard on ourselves,
and early, at dawn, in armour, having armed ourselves,
at the hollow ships we will rouse sharp Ares.
sentences.i: But for the night we shall guard ourselves, and early at dawn, armed in our gear, we shall rouse keen battle at the hollow ships.
sentences.n: The plan in two halves, night and dawn. ἐπὶ νυκτί is ‘for the night’, φυλάξομεν is ‘we shall guard’, and ἡμέας αὐτούς is ‘ourselves’. πρῶϊ is ‘early’ and ὑπηοῖοι ‘at dawn’; σὺν τεύχεσι is ‘with armour’, and θωρηχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of θωρήσσομαι, ‘having armed ourselves’. ἐγείρομεν, a short-vowel form, is read as a future, ‘we shall rouse’, and ὀξὺν Ἄρηα ‘sharp Ares’ is battle. νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ‘at the hollow ships’ has the accent drawn back.

sentences.t:
εἴσομαι εἴ κέ μ’ ὁ Τυδεΐδης κρατερὸς Διομήδης
πὰρ νηῶν πρὸς τεῖχος ἀπώσεται, ἤ κεν ἐγὼ τὸν
χαλκῷ δῃώσας ἔναρα βροτόεντα φέρωμαι.
sentences.l:
I shall know whether the son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes,
will thrust me from the ships to the wall, or I him,
having cut down with bronze, shall carry off the bloody spoils.
sentences.i: I shall find out whether Diomedes, the strong son of Tydeus, will thrust me back from the ships to the wall, or whether I shall cut him down with bronze and carry off his bloody spoils.
sentences.n: Hector names his rival. εἴσομαι is the future of οἶδα, ‘I shall know, find out’, and εἰ … ἀπώσεται … ἤ … φέρωμαι is a double question, ‘whether … or’. Τυδεΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Tydeus’, with κρατερὸς Διομήδης ‘strong Diomedes’. ἀπώσεται is the future middle of ἀπωθέω ‘thrust away’; τεῖχος ‘wall’ is not said to be Troy’s, though that is the natural sense. δῃώσας is the aorist participle of δηϊόω ‘cut down’, and ἔναρα βροτόεντα are ‘bloody spoils’ stripped from a slain man.

sentences.t:
αὔριον ἣν ἀρετὴν διαείσεται, εἴ κ’ ἐμὸν ἔγχος
μείνῃ ἐπερχόμενον·
sentences.l:
Tomorrow his own excellence he will discern, if my spear
will withstand him as he comes on;
sentences.i: Tomorrow he will discover his own excellence, if my spear stands firm against him as he comes on;
sentences.n: ἣν is the possessive ἑός ‘his own’ (written with a rough breathing), not the relative; ἀρετή is ‘excellence’, what makes a man good at fighting. διαείσεται is a future whose exact formation is not certain; it is taken to mean ‘will see through, discern’. εἴ κ’ … μείνῃ is ‘if … should withstand’, with the subjunctive, and ἐπερχόμενον ‘as he comes on’ is the accusative participle for Diomedes, the unstated object.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐν πρώτοισιν ὀΐω
κείσεται οὐτηθείς, πολέες δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι
ἠελίου ἀνιόντος ἐς αὔριον·
sentences.i: but I suspect he will lie among the foremost, wounded, with many of his companions round him, as the sun rises tomorrow;
sentences.n: Hector’s expectation: ἀλλά ‘but’ sets it against the doubt of the last unit. ὀΐω is ‘I suspect’ and κείσεται ‘will lie’, the subject, Diomedes, being unstated. οὐτηθείς is the aorist passive participle of οὐτάω ‘wound with a thrust’. πολέες is the epic form of πολλοί. ἠελίου ἀνιόντος is a genitive absolute, ‘the sun rising’, and ἐς αὔριον is ‘for tomorrow’, ‘on the morrow’.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼν ὣς
εἴην ἀθάνατος καὶ ἀγήρως ἤματα πάντα,
τιοίμην δ’ ὡς τίετ’ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἀπόλλων,
ὡς νῦν ἡμέρη ἥδε κακὸν φέρει Ἀργείοισιν.
sentences.l:
For if only I thus
were immortal and ageless all my days,
and were honoured as Athena and Apollo are honoured,
as this day now brings evil to the Argives.”
sentences.i: If only I were as surely immortal and ageless for all my days, and honoured as Athena and Apollo are honoured, as it is certain that this day now brings evil to the Argives.”
sentences.n: The speech ends in a wish. εἰ γάρ with the optative εἴην is ‘if only I were’, and the first ὣς (‘so’) is answered by the last, ὡς νῦν … ‘as surely as this day now brings evil’, while the middle ὡς τίετ’ is a separate ‘as … is honoured’. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. ἀθάνατος ‘immortal’ and ἀγήρως ‘ageless’ are different words. τιοίμην is the optative of τίω ‘honour’, in the passive sense ‘be honoured’, and τίετ’ is τίεται, ‘is honoured’. ἤματα πάντα is ‘all my days’.

sentences.t: ὣς Ἕκτωρ ἀγόρευ’, ἐπὶ δὲ Τρῶες κελάδησαν.
sentences.l: So Hector declared, and upon it the Trojans shouted.
sentences.i: So Hector spoke, and the Trojans shouted in response.
sentences.n: This is the usual closing line of an assembly speech: ὣς … ἀγόρευ’ (ἀγόρευε, elided) ‘so he declared’. ἐπὶ δὲ … κελάδησαν separates the preposition from its verb (tmesis), ‘shouted upon it’, that is, answered with a roar of approval. κελάδησαν is the aorist of κελαδέω ‘make a loud noise’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἵππους μὲν λῦσαν ὑπὸ ζυγοῦ ἱδρώοντας,
δῆσαν δ’ ἱμάντεσσι παρ’ ἅρμασιν οἷσιν ἕκαστος·
sentences.l:
And they the horses, on the one hand, unyoked from the yoke, sweating,
and bound them with straps beside their chariots, each man his own;
sentences.i: They unyoked their sweating horses from the yoke, and tied them with straps beside their chariots, each man by his own;
sentences.n: The Trojans carry out the orders. οἳ δέ is ‘and they’ (the article-form as a pronoun), and ἵππους μέν is answered by δῆσαν δέ; λῦσαν is the aorist of λύω, with ὑπὸ ζυγοῦ ‘from the yoke’. ἱδρώοντας ‘sweating’ is a participle agreeing with the horses. δῆσαν is the aorist of δέω ‘bind’, with ἱμάντεσσι ‘straps’ (epic dative -εσσι) and ἅρμασιν ‘chariots’. οἷσιν is the possessive ‘their own’, with ἕκαστος ‘each man’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ πόλιος δ’ ἄξοντο βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα
καρπαλίμως, οἶνον δὲ μελίφρονα οἰνίζοντο,
σῖτόν τ’ ἐκ μεγάρων, ἐπὶ δὲ ξύλα πολλὰ λέγοντο.
sentences.l:
and from the city they brought for themselves cattle and stout flocks
swiftly, and wine, honey-hearted, they got for themselves,
and food from the halls, and much wood they gathered besides.
sentences.i: and they brought cattle and stout flocks from the city, swiftly, and got themselves heart-sweetening wine and food from the halls, and gathered plenty of wood besides.
sentences.n: These three lines carry out Hector’s orders of 505–507 in the same words, with past indicatives (ἄξοντο, οἰνίζοντο, λέγοντο) where he had imperatives (ἄξεσθε, οἰνίζεσθε, λέγεσθε). The verbs are in the middle voice, ‘for themselves’, and the rest of the wording is unchanged, so the English is too, apart from the tense: the city supplies cattle and flocks, the halls supply wine and food, and the men gather wood.

sentences.t:
[ἔρδον δ’ ἀθανάτοισι τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας]
κνίσην δ’ ἐκ πεδίου ἄνεμοι φέρον οὐρανὸν εἴσω.
sentences.l:
and they were offering to the immortals complete hecatombs,
and the savour from the plain the winds bore up into heaven.
sentences.i: And they offered complete hecatombs to the immortals, and the winds bore the savour up from the plain into heaven.
sentences.n: Line 548 is printed in square brackets by the edition, which means that editors doubt it. ἔρδον is the imperfect of ἔρδω ‘offer, sacrifice’, with τεληέσσας ‘complete’ (the Odyssey’s epithet for hecatombs). κνίσην is the smell of burning fat, ‘savour’, the object of φέρον ‘bore’; ἄνεμοι ‘winds’ is the subject, ἐκ πεδίου ‘from the plain’, and οὐρανὸν εἴσω ‘into heaven’ has εἴσω after its noun.

sentences.t:
[ἡδεῖαν· τῆς δ’ οὔ τι θεοὶ μάκαρες δατέοντο,]
[οὐδ’ ἔθελον· μάλα γάρ σφιν ἀπήχθετο Ἴλιος ἱρή,]
[καὶ Πρίαμος καὶ λαὸς ἐϋμμελίω Πριάμοιο]
sentences.l:
sweet; but of it not at all did the blessed gods partake,
nor were they willing; for greatly to them was hateful sacred Ilium,
and Priam and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear.
sentences.i: It was sweet; but the blessed gods took no share of it, and had no wish to, for sacred Ilium was hateful to them, and Priam, and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear.
sentences.n: All three lines are printed in square brackets by the edition, which means that editors doubt them; they say that the gods refuse the Trojans’ sacrifice. ἡδεῖαν ‘sweet’ agrees with κνίσην; δατέοντο is the imperfect of δατέομαι ‘share, divide among themselves’, with the genitive τῆς ‘of it’. ἀπήχθετο is the aorist of ἀπεχθάνομαι ‘become hateful’, put as ‘was hateful’ as at 3.454. Line 552 repeats 4.47, where Zeus says that Priam and his people were honoured above all, and it ends without a stop in the edition.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ μέγα φρονέοντες ἐπὶ πτολέμοιο γεφύρας
εἴατο παννύχιοι, πυρὰ δέ σφισι καίετο πολλά.
sentences.l:
And they, thinking great thoughts, on the bridges of war
sat all night long, and for them fires were burning, many.
sentences.i: But they, high in spirit, sat all night long on the bridges of war, and many fires burned for them.
sentences.n: The Trojans bivouac in the field. μέγα φρονέοντες is ‘thinking big’, proud and confident. πτολέμοιο γεφύρας ‘the bridges of war’ is a figure the Greek does not explain, usually taken as the open ground between the armies. εἴατο is the plural of ἧμαι, ‘were sitting’, and παννύχιοι ‘all night long’ agrees with the subject. πυρά is ‘fires’, and καίετο is singular because a neuter plural takes a singular verb.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἐν οὐρανῷ ἄστρα φαεινὴν ἀμφὶ σελήνην
φαίνετ’ ἀριπρεπέα, ὅτε τ’ ἔπλετο νήνεμος αἰθήρ·
sentences.l:
And as when in heaven the stars about the shining moon
appear outstanding, when the upper air has become windless;
sentences.i: As when, in heaven, the stars appear outstanding around the shining moon, when the upper air has fallen windless;
sentences.n: A simile begins, with the usual ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’. ἄστρα ‘stars’ is the subject of φαίνετ’ (φαίνεται), ‘appear’, with ἀριπρεπέα ‘outstanding’ in agreement; ἀμφὶ σελήνην is ‘around the moon’. ὅτε τ’ ἔπλετο is ‘when it has become’, the aorist of πέλομαι, and νήνεμος is ‘windless’. αἰθήρ is the bright upper air, above the lower air.

sentences.t:
ἔκ τ’ ἔφανεν πᾶσαι σκοπιαὶ καὶ πρώονες ἄκροι
καὶ νάπαι·
sentences.l:
and there show forth all the look-outs and the high headlands
and the glens;
sentences.i: and all the look-out points show clear, and the high headlands and the glens;
sentences.n: ἔκ τ’ ἔφανεν is ἐξέφανεν, with the preposition separated from the verb; ἔφανεν is a plural, an epic aorist passive in -εν (for -ησαν), ‘came into view’, with πᾶσαι σκοπιαί ‘all the look-outs’ (peaks with a wide view) as the subject. πρώονες ἄκροι are ‘high headlands’, and νάπαι are wooded glens. All three are lit by the moon and stars when the air is still and clear.

sentences.t:
οὐρανόθεν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπερράγη ἄσπετος αἰθήρ,
πάντα δὲ εἴδεται ἄστρα, γέγηθε δέ τε φρένα ποιμήν·
sentences.l:
and from heaven is torn open the boundless upper air,
and all the stars are seen, and the shepherd rejoices in his mind;
sentences.i: and from heaven the boundless upper air bursts open, and every star is seen, and the shepherd is glad in his mind;
sentences.n: οὐρανόθεν is ‘from heaven’, with the ending -θεν. ὑπερράγη is the aorist passive of ὑπερρήγνυμι, ‘was burst open from above’, said of ἄσπετος αἰθήρ ‘the boundless upper air’; the sky seems to split and open. εἴδεται, from εἴδομαι, is ‘is seen’, ‘shows’. γέγηθε is a perfect with present force, ‘rejoices’, and φρένα is an accusative of respect, ‘in his mind’; δέ τε is a pair of particles for a general truth. The shepherd is the one who watches the night sky.

sentences.t:
τόσσα μεσηγὺ νεῶν ἠδὲ Ξάνθοιο ῥοάων
Τρώων καιόντων πυρὰ φαίνετο Ἰλιόθι πρό.
sentences.l:
so many, between the ships and the streams of Xanthus,
of the Trojans burning, fires were showing before Ilios.
sentences.i: So many fires, which the Trojans were burning, shone between the ships and the streams of Xanthus, in front of Ilios.
sentences.n: The simile’s other half: τόσσα ‘so many’ picks up the stars, and πυρά ‘fires’ is its noun. μεσηγύ is ‘between’, with the genitives νεῶν and ῥοάων ‘streams’ (the river Xanthus); Τρώων καιόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘the Trojans burning’. φαίνετο is ‘showed’, and Ἰλιόθι πρό is ‘in front of Ilios’, with -θι for ‘at’.

sentences.t:
χίλι’ ἄρ’ ἐν πεδίῳ πυρὰ καίετο, πὰρ δὲ ἑκάστῳ
εἴατο πεντήκοντα σέλᾳ πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο.
sentences.l:
A thousand fires then in the plain were burning, and beside each
sat fifty, in the gleam of blazing fire.
sentences.i: A thousand fires were burning in the plain, and beside each one sat fifty men in the gleam of the blazing fire.
sentences.n: The count: χίλι’ is χίλια ‘a thousand’, and καίετο is singular because a neuter plural takes a singular verb. πὰρ δὲ ἑκάστῳ is ‘and beside each’, and εἴατο ‘sat’ has no stated subject, so ‘fifty’ must mean fifty men (supplied here). σέλᾳ is the dative of σέλας ‘gleam’, with πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο ‘blazing fire’. The numbers are for effect: a thousand fires, fifty men at each, fifty thousand men.

sentences.t:
ἵπποι δὲ κρῖ λευκὸν ἐρεπτόμενοι καὶ ὀλύρας
ἑσταότες παρ’ ὄχεσφιν ἐΰθρονον Ἠῶ μίμνον.
sentences.l:
And the horses, feeding on white barley and spelt,
standing beside the chariots, awaited fair-throned Dawn.
sentences.i: And the horses, standing beside their chariots and feeding on white barley and spelt, waited for fair-throned Dawn.
sentences.n: The close of the book: horses wait with their masters. κρῖ ‘barley’ is a short, old neuter noun, and λευκόν ‘white’ goes with it; ὀλύρας is ‘spelt’, a kind of grain (the plant is not certain). ἐρεπτόμενοι ‘feeding on’ and ἑσταότες ‘standing’ are participles agreeing with ἵπποι. ὄχεσφιν has the ending -φιν (‘beside the chariots’). ἐΰθρονον Ἠῶ is ‘fair-throned Dawn’, the Odyssey’s epithet for her, and μίμνον ‘awaited’ is the imperfect of μίμνω.
